records.name: Arabian Sea
records.subtitle: Monsoon winds and changing productivity

sections.title: A northern Indian Ocean basin
sections.body: The Arabian Sea extends between the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, Pakistan and western India. Its open southern boundary connects it to the wider Indian Ocean, while adjoining gulfs and coastal shelves create varied conditions. The sea lies along routes that have connected communities for thousands of years. Its water and atmosphere are especially influenced by seasonal monsoon changes.

sections.title: The summer monsoon
sections.body: Winds change substantially through the year, influencing surface currents, waves and the mixing of seawater. In parts of the basin, upwelling brings cooler, nutrient-rich water towards the surface and supports plankton productivity. The pattern is not uniform across the entire sea. Researchers use satellite data and measurements of temperature and salinity to understand where seasonal processes are strongest.

sections.title: Marine food webs and oxygen
sections.body: Plankton forms the basis of ecosystems supporting fish and other animals, but the region also contains significant oxygen-poor waters at some depths. Organisms respond to both the availability of food and the chemistry of the water around them. Changing conditions can influence fisheries and marine habitats. Scientific monitoring matters because a change at the surface may not represent changes below.

sections.title: Ports and cultural exchange
sections.body: Maritime trade linked eastern Africa, Arabia and South Asia long before modern shipping. Sailors understood seasonal winds and used them to plan routes. Contemporary ports, fisheries and coastal settlements still depend on the sea. The Arabian Sea shows how atmospheric processes, ecology and human navigation can be connected, while climate change adds new uncertainties for communities around its shores.

records.quickFact: The Arabian Sea extends between the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, Pakistan and western India.

records.name: South China Sea
records.subtitle: A monsoon-driven marginal sea

sections.title: Water between Southeast Asian coasts
sections.body: The South China Sea lies between southern China, mainland Southeast Asia, Borneo and the Philippines. Straits and passages connect it with neighbouring seas and the Pacific and Indian Ocean systems. Shallow continental shelves contrast with deeper central waters. Islands, reefs and coastal wetlands add to the varied geography, making it misleading to describe the region as one unbroken shallow tropical sea.

sections.title: Seasonal circulation
sections.body: Northeasterly and southwesterly monsoon winds influence currents during different parts of the year. Scientists study how those changes affect sea-surface temperature, mixing and coastal upwelling. Conditions can vary substantially across the basin, especially near straits and shorelines. Weather systems and wider Pacific climate patterns can add variability beyond the normal seasonal cycle.

sections.title: Fishing and sensitive habitats
sections.body: The sea includes coral reefs, seagrass beds and productive coastal waters supporting many fisheries. Marine organisms move across political boundaries, while pollution and intense use can damage habitats. Some offshore areas are difficult to monitor. Management decisions need sound evidence about ecology rather than assumptions drawn from a map of islands or shipping routes alone.

sections.title: Navigation and disputed claims
sections.body: Major shipping routes cross the region and connect ports across Asia. Several governments maintain overlapping territorial and maritime claims; the wording used for particular features can therefore carry political implications. A geography article should distinguish uncontested physical processes from disputed boundaries and names. The sea is simultaneously an ecological system, a transport corridor and a focus of international legal disagreements.

records.quickFact: The South China Sea lies between southern China, mainland Southeast Asia, Borneo and the Philippines.

records.name: East China Sea
records.subtitle: River sediment and continental shelf waters

sections.title: A shelf sea off East Asia
sections.body: The East China Sea lies between the Chinese mainland, the Ryukyu island chain and neighbouring waters towards Taiwan, Japan and the Korean Peninsula. Much of it occupies a broad continental shelf. The large Chang Jiang, or Yangtze, river system brings freshwater and sediment to coastal waters, helping create strong contrasts between nearshore and offshore conditions.

sections.title: Currents and boundaries
sections.body: The Kuroshio Current flows near the outer eastern part of the region and transports warm Pacific water northwards. Tides, seasonal winds and river discharge interact with that broader circulation. These influences affect temperature, salinity and the movement of plankton and nutrients. The water does not behave as one uniform current that carries everything along the same route.

sections.title: Coasts and living resources
sections.body: Fisheries, ports and dense coastal populations connect the sea to economic activity. Estuaries and shelf habitats support many species, but nutrient input, pollution and heavy use can produce ecological pressures. Marine management is complicated by how rapidly a river plume or seasonal front can shift. Understanding the shelf means examining where fresh and saline water meet.

sections.title: Geography and differing names
sections.body: Some islands and maritime zones near the sea are subject to disputes among governments. These questions should be described separately from physical geography, without presenting contested claims as settled facts. The East China Sea provides an example of how a wide shallow shelf connects major river systems, ocean currents and heavily used coastlines.

records.quickFact: The East China Sea lies between the Chinese mainland, the Ryukyu island chain and neighbouring waters towards Taiwan, Japan and the Korean Peninsula.

records.name: Philippine Sea
records.subtitle: Deep trenches beside island arcs

sections.title: A deep sea east of the islands
sections.body: The Philippine Sea lies in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines and towards Taiwan, Japan and the Mariana island region. Its seafloor includes deep basins, ridges and trenches associated with plate tectonics. Some very deep ocean environments occur nearby, unlike the shallow coral shelves common along parts of the surrounding islands. The name refers to a marine region, not the territorial waters of one country.

sections.title: Tectonic boundaries
sections.body: Oceanic plates interact around the sea through subduction and other geological processes. Earthquakes, island arcs and trenches are linked to these movements over long periods. The seafloor is therefore neither flat nor static. Researchers map its shape and study sediments and rocks to investigate the evolution of the western Pacific, although large areas remain difficult to observe directly.

sections.title: Currents and open-ocean habitats
sections.body: Warm currents and atmospheric conditions affect surface water, while very deep regions contain habitats without sunlight. Marine food webs differ between productive coastal zones and open water. Animals may migrate across vast distances, and connectivity between habitats makes conservation planning challenging. It is misleading to judge the sea's biodiversity only by reef photographs from nearby islands.

sections.title: Research across boundaries
sections.body: Observations by ships, satellites and remotely operated vehicles help scientists investigate circulation, depth and marine organisms. Fisheries and maritime routes are important around its margins. The Philippine Sea offers a strong example of the difference between the familiar surface of an ocean and its much more complex geological structure beneath.

records.quickFact: The Philippine Sea lies in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines and towards Taiwan, Japan and the Mariana island region.

records.name: Coral Sea
records.subtitle: An ocean of reefs, cays and deep basins

sections.title: East of Australia's tropical coast
sections.body: The Coral Sea lies east of Queensland and includes extensive reefs, islands and deep water. The Great Barrier Reef forms a major coastal reef system on its western side, while offshore features extend far beyond it. The Australian Coral Sea Marine Park protects a large area of varied marine habitats, including coral structures, seamounts and deep plains.

sections.title: Life at different depths
sections.body: Sunlit reefs support abundant fish, invertebrates and other marine organisms. Farther offshore, water depths and food supply differ greatly, with deep habitats that cannot be understood from tropical reef photographs. Currents connect some populations across reefs and island groups. Species may depend on different areas during breeding, feeding and migration, making habitat connectivity important.

sections.title: Currents and seasonal weather
sections.body: Tropical weather systems, trade winds and ocean circulation influence waves and temperature. Coral reefs grow under particular environmental conditions and may be stressed by marine heatwaves and pollution. Reef-building animals are part of complex ecological communities rather than decorative rock formations. Conservation monitoring looks at changes in coral cover, water conditions and the organisms living among reef structures.

sections.title: Protecting a large marine region
sections.body: Marine parks restrict or regulate certain activities to conserve habitats, while offshore waters remain important for research and navigation. Managing such an extensive area requires surveillance and scientific evidence. The Coral Sea demonstrates that marine heritage extends well beyond the easily visited shore, and that protecting reef systems means considering ocean conditions across an enormous geographical scale.

records.quickFact: The Coral Sea lies east of Queensland and includes extensive reefs, islands and deep water.

records.name: Tasman Sea
records.subtitle: The changing ocean between Australia and New Zealand

sections.title: A sea between two countries
sections.body: The Tasman Sea lies between south-eastern Australia and New Zealand, connected with surrounding South Pacific and Southern Ocean waters. Its currents and water temperatures vary across latitude and season. Deep ocean water meets continental shelf habitats near the coasts, while storms can generate powerful waves. The sea is not one simple empty gap between two islands and a continent.

sections.title: Moving water and heat
sections.body: The East Australian Current transports relatively warm water along Australia's eastern margin and can produce large eddies in the Tasman region. These structures influence mixing and the distribution of heat and nutrients. Winds and changing weather patterns also affect surface circulation. Oceanographers combine satellites, floating instruments and vessels to understand the sea's shifting conditions.

sections.title: Marine life and coastal routes
sections.body: Fisheries and species moving over long distances connect different parts of the region. Seabirds, marine mammals and other organisms depend on both open water and productive coastal habitats. Their distribution may change with ocean conditions. Shipping and flights connect Australia and New Zealand today, but the marine environment has long shaped travel and scientific exploration.

sections.title: A link in the wider Pacific
sections.body: The Tasman Sea influences weather and ocean conditions along surrounding coasts. Temperature change, storms and marine heatwaves can affect ecosystems and people. Studying it demonstrates that water movement, atmospheric systems and regional geography interact, even where no obvious physical boundary separates the named sea from the broader ocean.

records.quickFact: The Tasman Sea lies between south-eastern Australia and New Zealand, connected with surrounding South Pacific and Southern Ocean waters.

records.name: Andaman Sea
records.subtitle: Islands, reefs and monsoon waters

sections.title: A tropical sea beside Southeast Asia
sections.body: The Andaman Sea lies west of Thailand and Myanmar, extending towards the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It connects with the Bay of Bengal and, through southern straits, neighbouring marine systems. Its shorelines include limestone islands, beaches, mangroves and productive coastal waters. Conditions differ between sheltered bays and deeper offshore regions.

sections.title: Reefs and diverse habitats
sections.body: The Surin and Similan island groups contain important coral ecosystems and support marine life associated with tropical waters. Reefs, seagrass and coastal environments offer food and habitat for different species. Seasonal upwelling and currents can influence nutrient availability. Conservation requires considering conditions beyond a single popular dive site, including the connected island and coastal environment.

sections.title: The monsoon and the sea
sections.body: Seasonal winds change wave conditions, currents and rainfall patterns. Those variations influence shipping, fishing and the movement of sediment around the coast. Underwater ecosystems may be affected by changing water temperatures and land-based runoff. Researchers monitor these conditions to understand ecological change rather than treating every season as identical.

sections.title: Communities and protection
sections.body: Fishing and maritime travel have long connected communities around the Andaman Sea. Tourism now contributes to local economies while placing pressure on reefs and coastal land. Marine reserves and national parks manage access to sensitive habitats, but the wider sea crosses several jurisdictions. Its story is best understood through the interaction between monsoons, island geology and living marine ecosystems.

records.quickFact: The Andaman Sea lies west of Thailand and Myanmar, extending towards the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

records.name: Labrador Sea
records.subtitle: Winter mixing in the North Atlantic

sections.title: Between Greenland and Canada
sections.body: The Labrador Sea lies in the North Atlantic between Greenland and the coast of Labrador. Cold air, ocean currents and seasonal ice conditions influence its surface waters. The sea connects shelf areas with deep ocean basins, making it an important place for studying North Atlantic circulation. It is not simply a cold coastal inlet; processes in its deeper waters affect a much larger region.

sections.title: The winter overturning process
sections.body: In some winters, intense cooling and changing water properties permit deep vertical mixing known as convection. Scientists use Argo floats and other observations to measure how deep this mixing reaches and how it changes between years. It helps form Labrador Sea Water, a water mass that moves into other Atlantic regions. The depth of mixing is not constant from one winter to the next.

sections.title: Oxygen and the deep ocean
sections.body: Convection can bring oxygen-rich surface water into deeper layers and influence conditions for marine life. Freshwater from melting ice and differences in atmospheric forcing can change the density structure. These processes are part of a wider ocean circulation system, but their exact effects require careful measurement. Researchers study temperature, salinity and dissolved gases together rather than relying on surface conditions alone.

sections.title: A link to distant climates
sections.body: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation transports water and heat over large distances. Labrador Sea processes contribute to understanding it, though they should not be reduced to a single switch that determines Europe's weather. The region is an excellent example of why a remote sea is important for global ocean science and long-term climate observations.

records.quickFact: The Labrador Sea lies in the North Atlantic between Greenland and the coast of Labrador.
